tldr: Bessent tells Nvidia's board to hire an outside CEO and gives it 10 days on export-control compliance.
Trump, Xi and Putin meet together for the first time Thursday in Shenzhen, with nuclear arms on the agenda.
China's October retail sales, factory output and investment all missed forecasts.
FDA rejects Summit's ivonescimab for lung cancer over the missing survival benefit.
Kansas City Fed's Schmid says inflation is running too hot; a December hike is fully priced.
Estonia will close every border crossing with Russia on December 1 after a GRU-linked arson attempt.
Anthropic prices its IPO Wednesday near a $1 trillion valuation, below earlier talk.
FDA approves Imfinzi with Padcev for bladder cancer patients who cannot take cisplatin.
DRAM price-fixing class action against Samsung, SK hynix and Micron survives dismissal.
Judge calls the administration's reasons for closing a DC golf course "transparently pretextual."

items.headline: Treasury secretary tells Nvidia's board to hire an outside CEO and prove it followed export rules
items.body: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on November 15 that Nvidia's board should bring in an outside chief executive, and gave the company 10 days to document its compliance with US export controls. The demand came four days after Jensen Huang resigned as CEO, president and director. Bessent also blamed Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick's department for the lapse, saying Treasury, State, Defense and the US Trade Representative had wanted the firm Megaspeed added to the export control list for months while Commerce held the file; the New York Times reported that Commerce had paused its investigation into whether Megaspeed helped route Nvidia chips to China. Bessent said Trump has drawn a line against selling China anything more advanced than Nvidia's H200, and opposed new chip legislation in favor of enforcing the rules that exist. Nvidia reports fiscal third-quarter results on November 17.
items.plain: Nvidia makes the chips that nearly every AI system runs on, and US law restricts which of them can be sold to China. Megaspeed is a company American officials suspect of buying those chips and passing them to Chinese buyers. Bessent, who runs the Treasury Department, is saying two things at once: that Nvidia may have looked the other way to keep sales up, and that the Commerce Department, which actually issues export licences, sat on the case. Nvidia's chief executive quit last week over a separate scandal, so the board is already hunting for a replacement, and Bessent wants that person to come from outside the company.
items.why: The fight is now between two cabinet departments over who lost control of chip exports, which makes the legislated licensing regime Bessent is trying to head off more likely rather than less.

items.headline: Trump, Xi and Putin will meet together for the first time on Thursday in Shenzhen
items.body: China's foreign ministry said on November 16 that Xi Jinping will host Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin for a trilateral meeting on November 19, on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen, describing the agenda as safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability. The White House and Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov have both confirmed it; it would be the first time the leaders of the three largest nuclear-armed states have sat down together. US officials said Trump wants to discuss reducing global nuclear arsenals and will raise the war with Iran, but is not expected to take up Ukraine, and one official played down the chance of any agreement, calling the meeting a first step. China has long insisted Washington and Moscow cut their own stockpiles before it discusses its own. Trump flies first to the Philippines for talks with Southeast Asian leaders.
items.plain: The US, Russia and China hold almost all of the world's nuclear weapons, and the treaties that used to cap the American and Russian arsenals have mostly lapsed. Trump wants a new deal covering all three countries. The catch is the arithmetic: the US and Russia each hold thousands of warheads and China has a few hundred, so Beijing's standing position is that it will not freeze its smaller stockpile while the other two keep much larger ones. That is why American officials are describing a first meeting rather than a negotiation. APEC is an annual Asia-Pacific economic summit, and is simply the reason all three leaders are in the same city.
items.why: Even a photograph of the three leaders as equals delivers the great-power parity Beijing has sought for a decade, which is a concession made before anyone sits down.

items.headline: China's October data missed on every major measure
items.body: China's National Bureau of Statistics reported on November 16 that retail sales rose 0.4% from a year earlier in October, below the 0.8% forecast and down from 1.1% in September. Industrial output grew 4.8% against an expected 5.3%, slowing from 5.5%, and fixed-asset investment fell 8.1% year to date, worse than September's 7.2% decline. Car sales dropped 21.4% as earlier trade-in subsidies stopped pulling purchases forward. The composition was uneven: semiconductor production rose 21.9% and industrial robot output 26.0%, while smartphone and personal computer output fell by double digits. Exports remain the main support for growth, and analysts at ING said Beijing is unlikely to add stimulus before year-end, though other commentary read the figures as strengthening the case for it.
items.plain: These three numbers are the standard monthly read on China's economy: what people bought, what factories made, and what companies and local governments spent on building things. All three came in weaker than economists expected. The collapse in car sales has a specific cause: the government had been paying people to trade in old vehicles, and when that money stopped, the buyers it had pulled forward into this year simply were not there. The split inside the factory numbers is the interesting part. Anything tied to chips and automation is booming, and anything a consumer would buy is shrinking.
items.why: A Chinese economy that can only grow by exporting more pushes the adjustment onto everyone else's trade balance at a moment when tariffs are already the main point of friction.

items.headline: FDA rejects Summit's lung cancer drug for lack of a survival benefit
items.body: Summit Therapeutics disclosed on November 15 that the FDA issued a complete response letter refusing to approve ivonescimab combined with platinum chemotherapy for EGFR-mutated, non-squamous non-small cell lung cancer in patients who had already received an EGFR inhibitor. The agency said substantial evidence of effectiveness was not established without a statistically significant improvement in overall survival. The Phase III HARMONi trial met its primary progression-free survival endpoint, with a median of 6.8 months versus 4.4 months in the control arm, but the overall survival analysis showed only a positive trend. Summit said the letter applies to this application and that HARMONi-3 and its other trials continue. It did not disclose what additional evidence the FDA requested or a resubmission timeline, and the letter itself is not public.
items.plain: Ivonescimab is a bispecific antibody, a drug engineered to grab two targets at once: here, a brake on the immune system and a signal tumours use to grow blood vessels. Drug approvals can rest on two different measures. Progression-free survival asks how long before the cancer grows again. Overall survival asks whether patients actually lived longer. Summit's trial won on the first and not the second, and the FDA has now said the first is not enough on its own. Several large drugmakers have paid billions for rights to similar two-target drugs, so this reads as a verdict on a whole class rather than one company.
items.why: The FDA has set overall survival as the bar for PD-1/VEGF bispecifics, which reprices the risk on every deal signed for that class in the past two years.

items.headline: A Fed official says inflation is running too hot as markets fully price a December rate increase
items.body: Kansas City Fed President Jeff Schmid said on November 15, at a credit union conference in Hawaii, that inflation is uncomfortably above the 2% price stability target and moving in the wrong direction, and that the Fed has both the tools and the responsibility to act. He rejected the idea that inflation is beyond the central bank's control. He did not explicitly call for another increase, and he does not vote on the FOMC this year. Futures markets are now fully priced for a quarter-point hike at the December meeting, with a small probability of a half-point move, after October CPI rose 0.4% month over month and producer prices reached a 6.5% annual rate, the highest in nearly four years. The Fed raised rates to 3.75%-4.00% in September and held in October.
items.plain: The Fed's job is to keep prices rising at about 2% a year. They are rising faster than that, so the Fed is doing the opposite of what it did for most of the past two years: raising interest rates instead of cutting them. Higher rates make borrowing more expensive, which slows spending, which is meant to slow prices. Schmid does not hold a vote this year, so his remarks matter as a signal of where committee thinking sits rather than as a decision. The next real test is the PCE inflation report due November 25.
items.why: A Fed tightening into an AI-driven capital spending boom is leaning on the one part of the economy currently doing the growing.

items.headline: Estonia will close all its border crossings with Russia after an arson attempt on a drone maker
items.body: Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said on November 16 that all Estonia-Russia border crossing points will close as of December 1. Prime Minister Kristen Michal said Russia's GRU military intelligence service ordered an attempted arson attack on Threod Systems, which manufactures reconnaissance and attack drones. The domestic security service KAPO accused the GRU of hiring the arsonists, and prosecutors said eight residents of Latvia were detained, with arrests sought for five. The three crossings, Narva, Koidula and Luhamaa, handled about 444,000 people and 35,000 vehicles in the first half of 2026. Estonia said the closure would reduce Moscow's ability to conduct hostile activity and limit sanctions circumvention. Russia's foreign ministry said it would verify the claims; some reports describe the closure as covering road crossings specifically rather than all crossings.
items.plain: Estonia is a NATO member of about 1.3 million people sharing a land border with Russia. Threod Systems is one of the companies supplying drones to Ukraine, which makes it a target. Estonian investigators say the people who tried to set the factory alight were recruited and paid from abroad rather than being Russian officers themselves, a pattern several European countries have reported over the past two years. Closing the border is a sanctions measure as much as a security one, because it shuts a route that goods and people have used to get around trade restrictions.
items.why: Each closure removes another low-level channel between NATO and Russia, leaving fewer routine ways to defuse the next border incident.

items.headline: Anthropic's IPO prices Wednesday at a valuation near $1 trillion
items.body: Anthropic is scheduled to price its initial public offering on November 18 and begin trading on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT on November 19, selling about 801.4 million Class A shares at $70 to $78 each. Reuters put the implied valuation at up to $1.02 trillion on expected shares outstanding, while CNN reported roughly $1.4 trillion fully diluted at the top of the range; the gap is a counting difference, not a disagreement about the price. The public sale could raise about $64.4 billion, with a separate $26 billion private placement bringing the total to roughly $90.4 billion. The range sits below the $1.5 trillion figure discussed before this month's selloff in AI-linked stocks. Anthropic separately agreed in late September to pay about $3.4 billion for 1.7 gigawatts of gas-fired generators, which the Financial Times called the largest known purchase of power-generation equipment by an AI lab.
items.plain: An IPO is the moment a private company first sells shares to the public, and the price range is its best guess at what buyers will pay. Two valuation numbers are circulating because they count different things: one counts the shares that exist now, the other adds shares that employees and investors can convert later. The generator deal explains part of why the company needs the money. Chips are useless without electricity, and the grid cannot connect new data centres fast enough, so Anthropic bought its own gas turbines rather than wait years in a queue.
items.why: Pricing below the number discussed a month ago hands the market a public, daily quote on AI valuations that private funding rounds never provided.

items.headline: FDA clears AstraZeneca's Imfinzi with Padcev for bladder cancer patients who cannot take chemotherapy
items.body: The FDA approved durvalumab (Imfinzi) with enfortumab vedotin (Padcev) for adults with muscle-invasive bladder cancer who are ineligible for, or decline, cisplatin-based chemotherapy. AstraZeneca announced the approval on November 13. The regimen is three cycles of the combination before surgery followed by up to nine cycles of durvalumab alone after bladder removal, and it rests on the Phase III VOLGA trial, which showed statistically significant improvements in event-free survival and overall survival. AstraZeneca said the combination almost halved the risk of recurrence and cut the risk of death by 42%, a figure from the company's own statement. The clearance came under priority review, reported as six weeks ahead of the FDA's goal date, and is AstraZeneca's third bladder cancer indication in roughly two years. VOLGA-based applications are under review in the EU, Japan and elsewhere.
items.plain: Muscle-invasive bladder cancer has grown into the wall of the bladder, and the standard treatment has been chemotherapy built around a drug called cisplatin, followed by surgery to remove the bladder. A large share of these patients cannot take cisplatin, because it is hard on the kidneys and many of them are older with reduced kidney function, so until now their options were worse. This approval gives that group a regimen built from an immune-system drug and a targeted one instead. Note that the headline 42% figure comes from AstraZeneca describing its own trial.
items.why: Cisplatin-ineligible patients are the group oncology keeps leaving behind, and filling that gap turns a trial result into the default treatment for people who previously had nothing that worked as well.

items.headline: Judge lets a memory-chip price-fixing class action against Samsung, SK hynix and Micron go forward
items.body: US District Judge Noel Wise denied in full the three companies' joint motion to dismiss Garciaguirre v. Samsung Electronics on November 14, finding the complaint plausibly alleges an agreement in restraint of trade under Section 1 of the Sherman Act. Seventeen consumers and small businesses filed the suit on June 25, 2026, alleging the three manufacturers, which together supply most of the world's DRAM, cut production of the conventional memory used in laptops, phones and servers while shifting capacity to high-bandwidth memory for AI accelerators. Wise distinguished the case from a 2018 suit that was dismissed, citing newer alleged conduct including long-term HBM contracts, a refusal to sign long-term deals with conventional DRAM buyers, and Micron's shutdown of its Crucial consumer brand. The ruling is a pleading-stage decision, not a finding of liability, and moves the case into discovery.
items.plain: DRAM is the working memory in every computer and phone, and three companies make almost all of it. The claim is not that they raised prices directly, but that they made less of the ordinary kind because the version used in AI chips sells for far more. Less supply means higher prices, and memory prices have risen sharply this year. The judge has not decided whether any of this was coordinated. He has only said the accusation is specific enough to be tested. Discovery is the stage where plaintiffs get to read the companies' internal emails and planning documents.
items.why: Discovery will produce the first documentary record of how the AI buildout was allocated inside the memory industry, whatever the case's eventual outcome.

items.headline: A judge blocked the closure of a public DC golf course and called the administration's stated reasons pretextual
items.body: US District Judge Ana Reyes issued a temporary restraining order on November 14, one day before East Potomac Park was set to close, barring the Interior Department from shutting the park through at least November 28 while she considers a suit by the DC Preservation League. The department's closure notice had cited “numerous safety concerns due to their poor condition” and a lack of “operational management.” Reyes found those reasons “transparently pretextual,” noting that the administration had itself terminated the National Links Trust's operation of the course and then cited the absence of an operator as grounds to close it. She wrote that “President Trump directed this closure for one reason: so that work could begin on a new Fazio Design to replace the current East Potomac Golf Course,” and described the government's account to the court as “incomplete, if not misleading by omission” for leaving out that directive. She found the department likely violated at least the National Environmental Policy Act and the Administrative Procedure Act. Trump said on Truth Social that Interior would appeal, referring to the site as “Trash Island.” The order does not require the government to operate the course for play.
items.plain: East Potomac is a public golf course on federal parkland in Washington that has been open since the 1920s. The administration said it had to close for safety reasons and because nobody was running it, but the government had ended the operator's contract itself, which the judge treated as manufacturing the very problem it then cited. A temporary restraining order is a short pause rather than a final ruling; it lasts about two weeks while the court examines the case properly. What undercut the government's argument was its own paperwork and the president's public posts, which described a redevelopment plan his lawyers had not mentioned to the court.
items.why: Courts have repeatedly found this administration's stated rationales pretextual, and each such finding makes the next agency filing less likely to be taken at face value.
